# STARRY OBSERVATIONS

you encounter a gathering. Furthermore (which is more wonderful), the stars that have been called "nebulae" by astronomers down to this day are actually groups of stars gathered in a wonderful manner. From the mixing of their rays, while each individual star escapes the keenness of our eyes due to its smallness or its extreme distance from us, that brightness arises which, until now, has been believed to be a denser part of the sky capable of reflecting the rays of the stars or the Sun. We have observed several of them; and we have wished to append the star patterns of two.

In the first, you have the nebula called the Head of Orion, in which we have counted twenty-one stars.

The second contains the nebula called Praesepe <note>the Beehive Cluster</note>, which is not just one star, but a mass of more than forty stars: besides the Aselli <note>the 'Donkeys', two stars flanking the cluster</note>, we have noted thirty-six arranged in the following order.

->NEBULA PRAESEPE.<-

<note>A telescopic star chart of the 'Nebulosa Praesepe' (Beehive Cluster), depicting over thirty-six stars including the Aselli, providing pivotal evidence that this nebula is a dense star cluster.</note>

<column-break/>

->NEBULA OF ORION.<-

<note>A telescopic star chart of the 'Nebulosa Orionis' (Orion Nebula), showing twenty-one individual stars, representing one of the first telescopic proofs that such nebulous regions are composed of distinct stars.</note>

<summary>Galileo presents observations demonstrating that the celestial phenomena previously classified as nebulae are actually dense clusters of individual stars, specifically detailing his findings regarding the Orion nebula and the Praesepe cluster.</summary>
<keywords>Sidereus Nuncius, nebulae, Orion Nebula, Praesepe, Beehive Cluster, telescopic observation, Galileo Galilei</keywords>
